## Overview and objectives

Once the data has been downloaded and loaded using `clim4health_load`, several transformations can be applied to the data depending on the needs of the specific application. The objetive of this tutorial is to show the use `clim4health_spatial` function for spatial aggregation of climate products into polygon geometries.

<br>

![](./figures/general/clim4health_structure.png)

<br>


`clim4health_spatial` works with *s2dv_cube* objects and different types of climate data, for more background information please check the `clim4health_load`  tutorial. To follow this tutorial, please clone the repository and change directory to the project's root.


## 1. Setup

First of all, let's check whether all the necessary dependencies are available and if not,
install them:

```R
# Requirements for clim4health_load
if (!requireNamespace("startR", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("startR")
if (!requireNamespace("lubridate", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("lubridate")
if (!requireNamespace("easyNCDF", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("easyNCDF")
if (!requireNamespace("CSTools", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("CSTools")

# Requirements for clim4health_spatial
if (!requireNamespace("exactextractr", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("exactextractr")
```


Next, we source the *clim4health_load* and *clim4health_spatial* functions 
(make sure that the working directory is set to the path where the clim4health 
repository has been cloned).

```R
# Obtain the current working directory
clim4health_path <- getwd()

# Source the required functions to load and transform data.
source(paste0(clim4health_path, '/functions/clim4health_load.R'))
source(paste0(clim4health_path, '/functions/clim4health_spatial.R'))
```

## 2. Loading data

We use `clim4health_load` with available temperature data to load temperature 
reanalyses and forecasts into memory as *s2dv_cube* objects.

```r
# Reanalysis data (observations)
obs_path <- paste0(clim4health_path, "/sample_data/era5land/")

obs <- clim4health_load(obs_path, var = "t2m", data_type = "obs",
                         sdates = c("201004", "201005"), ext = "nc")
dim(obs$data)
#  dataset       var      time  ensemble  latitude longitude 
#        1         1         2         1       561       761 

# Forecast data 
fcst_path <- paste0(clim4health_path, "/sample_data/ecmwf51/forecast/")
fcst <- clim4health_load(fcst_path, var = "t2m", data_type = "fcst",
                         sdates = c("20240401"), ext = "nc")
dim(fcst$data)
#  dataset       var      time  ensemble  latitude longitude 
#        1         1         3        51        57        77 
```
Next, we specify the path to the vector data containing polygon geometries for
which we want to aggregate, which in our case is a shapefile.

```r
shp_file <- paste0(clim4health_path, "/sample_data/shapefiles/MGN_ANM_MPIOS.shp")
```

## 3. Spatially aggregating the data

To produce the spatial aggregation, we simply pass the *s2dv_cube* object and the path
to the file containing the polygons for the extraction to `clim4health_spatial`. 
The function will convert the cube into a georeferenced raster from which the intersecting
cells are extracted and summarised using a function (by default the mean).

```r
# Run it with the observations
result_obs  <- clim4health_spatial(obs, shp_file, agg_fun = "mean")

class(result_obs)
# [1] "s2dv_cube"

# Run it with the forecast
result_fcst <- clim4health_spatial(fcst, shp_file)

dim(result_obs$data)
#  dataset      var     time ensemble   region 
#        1        1        2        1     1122 

dim(result_fcst$data)
#  dataset      var     time ensemble   region 
#        1        1        3       51     1122 
```
